children: India’s defence industry is shifting from domestic capacity building to innovation-led growth, deeper private-sector participation and a stronger push into global markets

India's defence sector is entering a new phase. Over the past decade the country has built a stronger domestic industrial base, opened the door wider to private-sector players and pushed further into global defence markets. The question now is whether that foundation can turn into sustained capability, real innovation and lasting global competitiveness.

The numbers make the case. India's defence production hit a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in FY2025-26, and exports reached Rs 38,424 crore, with Indian defence products now reaching more than 80 countries. The government wants annual production at Rs 3 lakh crore and exports at Rs 50,000 crore by 2029. That target reframes the conversation: it's no longer just about building a domestic defence industry, but about making that industry innovative and competitive enough to serve both domestic and global demand.
Scaling the ecosystem

The defence ecosystem today includes public-sector organisations, private companies, MSMEs and technology-led enterprises, each working different parts of the value chain. The private sector accounted for 24% of defence production in FY2025-26, its highest share yet, and contributed 45.16% of exports, proof of how much ground it's covered in reaching international markets.

The next step is deepening that participation: stronger supply chains, more investment in specialised capabilities, and closer collaboration between big companies, MSMEs, research institutions and the armed forces. Scaling isn't just about producing more. It means building deeper expertise and capabilities that can hold up outside the domestic market, not just inside it.
Innovation will decide the next phase

Defence requirements are shifting fast, driven by new technology and a changing security landscape, which means continuous investment in research and development matters more than sticking with established manufacturing models.

The government raised R&D allocation to Rs 29,100.25 crore for 2026-27, more than double what it was in 2014-15, and set aside Rs 1.39 lakh crore in the defence budget for procurement from domestic industry. That's real room for Indian companies to develop and scale new capabilities. The harder part is making sure research actually turns into deployable products rather than staying on the shelf.

That shift from research to deployable capability is already visible, and it's worth naming where. In precision-guided munitions, the DRDO-Russia BrahMos supersonic cruise missile remains India's flagship, and it has moved beyond a single showcase deal into a genuine export line, with the Philippines, Vietnam and Indonesia among the international customers now on board.

The DRDO-developed Astra air-to-air missile and the Pinaka multi-barrel rocket system, including its longer-range guided variant, have followed a similar path from indigenous development to export interest, with Armenia already a Pinaka customer and other countries evaluating the system. Strategic missile production is also opening up to private industry, with systems such as Astra Mk-2 and the Pralay tactical ballistic missile positioned to anchor India's proposed Integrated Rocket Force.

Air defence tells the same story. The indigenous Akash system, and its higher-altitude Akash Prime and longer-range Akash-NG variants, were developed by DRDO with production and integration support from Bharat Dynamics and Bharat Electronics, and Akash has already secured its first overseas buyer.

More striking is what sits behind these missiles: Akashteer, the fully indigenous, AI-enabled air defence control and reporting system built by Bharat Electronics with DRDO and ISRO, which fuses radars, sensors and weapons into a single real-time picture for army air defence units. Its performance during recent operations has pushed it from a domestic command-and-control tool toward genuine export interest, including reported discussions with the UAE.

That points to the deeper capability India is now building: C5ISR, the layer of command, control, communications, computers, cyber, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance that lets separate weapons and sensors act as one networked force. Akashteer's ability to link with the Air Force's IACCS and the Navy's TRIGUN, and to integrate radars and weapons of Russian and Western origin on a single automated network, is as significant as any individual missile system.

The networking layer behind that is being built indigenously across the ecosystem: DRDO on the architecture, PSUs like Bharat Electronics and Bharat Dynamics on integration and production, and private players on the communication links that hold it together.

At Avantel, that has meant satellite communication terminals, software defined radios and HF systems that carry sensor and command traffic between ships, aircraft, ground stations and headquarters, and the ground segment infrastructure that lets dispersed platforms exchange data over a common backbone rather than through stovepiped systems. It's this connective tissue, as much as the sensors and shooters at either end, that turns a collection of platforms into a coherent, exportable capability rather than a set of disconnected wins.
From domestic demand to global markets

Export growth to Rs 38,424 crore in FY2025-26 shows Indian defence products are finding buyers abroad. Building on that means competing on technology, quality, reliability and cost, not just landing one-off deals.

Indian companies will need to think past individual export wins toward long-term capability: stronger partnerships, product development investment, global certifications and after-sales support as they expand internationally.
Building an ecosystem that's ready for what's next

The next decade calls for a wider approach. India needs continued investment in research and talent, tighter links between industry, academia, startups and the armed forces, and procurement processes that let new technologies move faster from development to deployment

The draft Defence Acquisition Procedure 2026 points in that direction, with proposed changes meant to strengthen indigenous design and development and push indigenous content higher. The goal isn't simply making more defence equipment. It's building an ecosystem that keeps developing, improving and getting new capabilities to market.
The next chapter

India spent the last decade building the foundations of a domestic defence industry. The next phase is about making those foundations deliver at real scale, moving from capacity to capability, from production to innovation, from domestic demand to global reach.

India's defence industry has the scale now to aim higher. What comes next depends on building the technology, talent, partnerships and market access to turn that scale into competitiveness that lasts, measured less by how much the country produces and more by how well it can innovate, scale and compete globally.
Siddhartha Abburi
Guest Author Siddhartha Abburi is Director at Avantel Limited.
